```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("theme.R")
library(housepi)
```

In this vignette we show how to compute common household measures according to the model posterior distribution.
This can is generally refered to as Posterior Predictive Checks (PPC).
We use the same chain binomial example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
# repeat inference as in vignette 'Get Started'
set.seed(42)
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("chain_binomial") |>
  add_data_wide(housepi::survey) |>
  load_parameter_list(alpha = list(prior = "uniform", proposal = "lognormal"),
                      beta = list(prior = "uniform", proposal = "lognormal"))

# estimate parameters
results <- hhmodel |>
  infer(steps = 3000, burnin = 1000, thin = 5,
        adapt = 2000, chains = 3, threads = 1, progress = FALSE)
estimates <- get_param_draws(results) |>
  posterior::summarise_draws()
estimates
```

## Predicted cases by size 

We can use the simulation process to challenge the validity of the inferred model on top of the original dataset.
We do so by computing the predicted numbers of cases per household size according to our posterior distribution (i. e. by producing simulations according to posterior values).

```{r}
# run simulations according to posterior traces to compute predictions
ppc <- predicted_cases_by_house_size(hhmodel, results, progress = FALSE)
```

To show both observed and predicted cases by size, we can extract the formatted cases table from our output object as follows.

```{r}
# for this part of the analysis we consider only house sizes up to 5
ppc$set_max_house_size(5)

# return a data.frame with observed and predicted cases
cases_df <- ppc$formatted_cases_table

# format predicted cases
combined <- cases_df$mean
mask_pred <- cases_df$mean$distr == "Predicted"
mask_cols <- setdiff(names(cases_df$mean), c("house_size", "distr"))

# format mean with its lower and upper credible interval bounds
combined[mask_pred, mask_cols] <- format_credible_intervals(
  cases_df$mean[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q5[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q95[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  as_integer = TRUE
)

# avoid separate_header regular expression to split house_size
names(combined)[names(combined) == "house_size"] <- "size"

# generate cases by household size table
flextable::flextable(combined) |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ size, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ size) |>
  flextable::align(align = "center", , part = "all") |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(size = "Size",
                                  distr = "Distribution",
                                  cases = "Number of Cases")) |>
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 12, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

We can perform a Chi-Squared test on the shown distribution as follows:

```{r}
# perform a Chi-Squared test
ppc$chisq_test()
```

The $p$-value tells us that there is no significant difference between the distribution, thus we can trust our inference process.

## Secondary attack rate

We can have a quick look at secondary attack rates of observed vs predicted cases using the fields `$sar`:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| waring: false

# we drop maximum house size before proceeding
ppc$drop_max_house_size()

library(ggplot2)

col_dict <- c(Predicted = "coral", Observed = "black")

# extract values for secondary attack rate
ggplot(ppc$formatted_sec_attack_rate, aes(x = house_size)) +
  # predicted SAR
  geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "Predicted")) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = mean, ymin = q5, ymax = q95, color = "Predicted"),
                width = 0.1) +
  # observed SAR
  geom_point(aes(y = observed, color = "Observed")) +
  # annotate observed counts
  geom_text(aes(x = house_size + 0.3, y = observed, 
                label = sprintf("[%s]", counts)),
            color = col_dict["Observed"]) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_dict) +
  labs(x = "Household Size", y = "Secondary Attack Rate", color = "")
```
